before: A graphical user interface (GUI) agent needs to establish that a requested control is present and uniquely identified before deciding where to click. We examine the native scores returned by a pinned visual interface, Jev 1.14: a visible-presence probability, a match-count distribution and one bounding box per request. These scores form the basis of frozen selective-execution policies. Presence and uniqueness gates made no incorrect accepted clicks on held-out synthetic layouts. The result did not carry over to real interfaces. A source audit found that 200 of the 951 human-labelled cases reused pilot screenshots. Among the 751 independent real-interface cases, the three-signal policy accepted 26 with a conditional risk of 61.5%; the frozen logistic gate accepted one. Strict localization succeeded on 41 of 131 unique targets (31.3%), limiting any gate to about 6.1% coverage at 10% accepted-error risk. Recalibration on real data improved Brier loss, but no threshold met the 10% risk target. A quantized Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline tested on matched inputs achieved 16.8% strict accuracy. We contribute a reproducible audit of transfer failure, the dependence of safety metrics on their denominators, and cohort provenance. We do not introduce a new uncertainty-control algorithm.
after: Before a graphical user interface (GUI) agent clicks, it must check that the requested control is present. It must also identify that control uniquely. We test frozen selective-execution policies using the native outputs of a pinned visual interface, Jev 1.14. For each request, it returns a visible-presence probability, a match-count distribution and one bounding box. Presence and uniqueness gates made no incorrect accepted clicks on held-out synthetic layouts. The result did not carry over to real interfaces. A source audit found that 200 of the 951 human-labelled cases reused pilot screenshots. Among the 751 independent real-interface cases, the three-signal policy accepted 26 with a conditional risk of 61.5%; the frozen logistic gate accepted one. Strict localization succeeded on 41 of 131 unique targets (31.3%), limiting any gate to about 6.1% coverage at 10% accepted-error risk. Recalibration on real data improved Brier loss, but no threshold met the 10% risk target. A quantized Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline tested on matched inputs achieved 16.8% strict accuracy. Our audit documents the transfer failure and cohort provenance. It also shows how the denominators affect the interpretation of safety metrics. We do not introduce a new uncertainty-control algorithm.

after: Here π̂_corr = 41/751 = 0.0546, so even an oracle gate is bounded by 0.0546/0.90 ≈ 6.1% coverage at α = 0.10 (Figure 3). The bound is deterministic and applies to this finite cohort. It gives no population guarantee and sets no ceiling on human performance. It changes if the grounder or scoring rule changes.

before: Probability quality. Original E has a Brier loss of 0.06125. The retrospective constant-prevalence predictor does better at 0.05234, leaving E with Brier skill −0.170 (Equation C1). Its low expected calibration error (ECE) is therefore insufficient evidence of useful probabilities. Nor do the extra native signals show strong additional discrimination: B and E have nearly the same AUROC, with overlapping source-cluster intervals on the real cohort. Appendix C.2 reports the ranking and Brier results in full.
after: Probability quality. Original E has a Brier loss of 0.06125, compared with 0.05234 for the retrospective constant-prevalence predictor. E therefore has a Brier skill of −0.170 (Equation C1). Its low expected calibration error (ECE) does not, on its own, show that the probabilities are useful. The extra native signals also add little discrimination. On the real cohort, B and E have nearly the same AUROC, and their source-cluster intervals overlap. The full ranking and Brier results appear in Appendix C.2.

before: On authored synthetic layouts, native presence and uniqueness signals substantially improve selective clicking. The real-interface results do not establish comparable usefulness. Once the 200 reused pilot cases are removed, the frozen logistic gate accepts only one of 751 real cases, while conditional risk for the three-signal policy is still 61.5%. What the study supports is a reproducible account of failed transfer, cohort provenance and safety metrics whose interpretation depends on the denominator. Under the tested interface, the quantized Qwen baseline has weaker strict localization, and neither model’s semantic one-label rule provides reliable acceptance. We have not established broader model superiority, formal safety or practical utility.
after: Native presence and uniqueness signals substantially improve selective clicking on authored synthetic layouts. We do not find comparable evidence of usefulness on real interfaces. After removing the 200 reused pilot cases, the frozen logistic gate accepts just one of 751 real cases. The three-signal policy still has a conditional risk of 61.5%. The study documents this failure to transfer, traces the cohort provenance and shows how denominators affect the interpretation of safety metrics. In tests with the same interface, the quantized Qwen baseline has lower strict localization accuracy. For both models, acceptance remains unreliable under the semantic one-label rule. These results do not establish broader model superiority, formal safety or practical utility.

before: Both annotators label 98 real cases unique. Across these cases, mean IoU between their boxes is 0.512. The boxes meet IoU ≥ 0.3 in 79.6% of cases, IoU ≥ 0.5 in 61.2%, and IoU ≥ 0.75 in 19.4%. A’s box centre falls within B’s box in 81.6%; reversing the direction gives 88.8%. These agreement rates provide a conditional annotation reference. They exclude status disagreements, use no independently verified true boxes, and cannot define an absolute ceiling for either humans or models.
after: Both annotators label 98 real cases unique. Their boxes have a mean IoU of 0.512 across these cases. IoU is at least 0.3 in 79.6% of cases, at least 0.5 in 61.2%, and at least 0.75 in 19.4%. A’s box centre lies inside B’s box in 81.6% of cases. B’s box centre lies inside A’s in 88.8%. These rates give a conditional reference for annotation agreement. They exclude cases in which the annotators disagree on status, and there are no independently verified true boxes. They therefore set no absolute ceiling on human or model performance.
